transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendoza (ForgeBank Head of Infra), Priya Sharma (ML Eng Lead), Liam O'Connor (Security Architect)
Shared: Redwood Dedicated deck (link), security packet (link)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Customer exploring Redwood Dedicated reserved GPU capacity for customer-facing LLM features. Key concerns: isolation/data residency, burst capacity for spikey traffic, autoscaling expectations, latency targets vs cost, compliance (SOC2, KMS, audit logs), and feasibility of on-prem/private later. Redwood to send pricing and run benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with me is Ethan our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Carlos Mendoza: Good, thanks. Carlos here. We, um, we've been evaluating options, we wanted to dig into Dedicated vs Hosted.
[00:10] Priya Sharma: Hey, Priya here, yeah we have production traffic now and starting to hit cost/latency constraints.
[00:14] Ethan Park: Awesome. Quick agenda, we'll do a quick intro, then go into your current infra and workload, sizing, isolation and compliance questions, then discuss Redwood Dedicated sizing and burst options, and finish with next steps. Sound good?
[00:22] Carlos: Yep.
[00:24] Liam O'Connor: Yup.
[00:26] Priya: Go for it.

[00:30] Ethan Park: Cool. Priya, can you summarize current usage? Peak QPS, average tokens per request, seq lengths, model types you run?
[00:39] Priya: Sure, so our main stuff is a customer support assistant and an intelligent routing layer. Peak QPS is about 120 req/s for the assistant during business hours, average request is around 350 tokens, 95th around 900 tokens. We run a mix of an open Chat model (we call it gpt-open-ish internally) and a lighter retrieval-augmented transformer for some routing decisions.
[00:58] Maya Chen: When you say 120 req/s that's all app servers combined?
[01:01] Priya: Yeah that's total across our fleet hitting the inference endpoints, with spikes up to 200 for flash promos or outages.
[01:07] Carlos: Cost has been creeping up with hosted endpoints and also we want isolation and legal contract for data residency for EU customers.
[01:13] Ethan Park: Great context. For Dedicated we offer reserved GPU pools to guarantee throughput, and you can configure burst capacity—basically a configurable burst pool to handle short spikes. The key tradeoff is reserved baseline cost vs the cost of burst usage.
[01:25] Priya: How does burst work? Is it instant? Do we need to pre-warm?
[01:29] Ethan Park: Burst is near-instant, it's limited by available burst quota and the GPU start-up time for cold nodes. We do keep a small hot warm pool to avoid cold-start latency, and for very predictable spikes we recommend scheduled autoscale policies. For abrupt very large spikes we fall back to compatible model variants or lower-precision quantized variants to avoid queuing—so graceful degradation.
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: For compliance: do you support VPC peering / Private deployments? We need to know about KMS integration and audit logs.
[01:52] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) is an option, but for most customers Dedicated can be deployed in a private network with customer-managed VPC peering and KMS integration. We support customer KMS/HSM for key wrap and we emit audit logs for all inference requests and admin actions. We'll share the security packet with specifics.
[02:05] Carlos: Is there an SLA for Dedicated?
[02:08] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and uptime targets aligned to the reserved capacity commitment. We'll include the SLA tier details in the pricing doc.
[02:14] Priya: For model ops, how do you handle model versioning and rollouts? We need pins per customer and canary testing.
[02:20] Ethan Park: We have model version pinning and rollout features—canary and A/B. You can route a % of traffic to a new model variant. Also automatic fallback policies to older model variants if latency or error rates rise.
[02:31] Priya: Good. For the quantization and perf: do you support INT8 / 4-bit and what kind of perf uplift?
[02:36] Ethan Park: We support quantization-friendly execution paths, Q8/Q4 depending on model architecture, with typical throughput up to 2–3x for Q4 vs FP16 for some models, but you trade off some quality. We'll recommend quant profiles per workload as part of Redwood Optimize.
[02:50] Carlos: Network egress and multi-region: we must keep EU traffic inside EU datacenters. Do you do region pinning?
[02:56] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing supports region pinning and policy routing by customer region. We can deploy Dedicated pools in EU regions for your EU tenant.
[03:03] Liam: Encryption at rest and in transit? Key rotation?
[03:06] Maya: Data in transit is TLS, at rest is encrypted with customer KMS if requested, and we support key rotation. Audit logs are immutable and can be exported to your SIEM.
[03:14] Priya: About throughput: how many tokens/sec can one GPU handle? We're trying to map from our QPS and seq lengths to GPU count.
[03:21] Ethan: It depends heavily on model, sequence length, and batching. As a rough ballpark: for a Llama-2-like 13B with FP16 on an A100, you might get ~200–300 tokens/sec per GPU at low latency settings, but with batching and KV cache reuse for chat histories that can increase. For larger models or stricter latency targets it's lower. We'll run a short benchmark with your sample prompts to produce a recommended GPU count.
[03:42] Carlos: Do you do continuous batching or does the app have to implement batching?
[03:45] Ethan: Runtime does continuous batching automatically, you can also do request-side batching. Continuous batching groups requests based on latency SLOs—so you get the benefit without adding complexity.
[03:53] Priya: If we have long-running chat sessions, how do you manage KV cache memory? Will that increase GPU memory requirements per seat?
[03:59] Ethan: Yes, KV cache grows with sequence length per session. We support offloading, segmented cache, and pool sizing to manage memory. For heavy chat workloads we recommend larger GPU memory SKUs (like H100 or higher mem variants) or more horizontal shards. We'll include options in the sizing doc.
[04:14] Carlos: On billing: is dedicated billed as committed monthly plus overage for burst?
[04:18] Maya: Typically reserved capacity is a committed monthly fee based on GPU hours and tier, and burst is billed when you exceed burst quota. There are multiple pricing profiles (committed-only, committed+burst, or committed with autoscale credits). We'll include concrete numbers in the pricing sheet.
[04:32] Liam: For legal and procurement, we need SOC2 report, ISO if available, and a data processing addendum (DPA).
[04:37] Maya: We'll share SOC2 and standard DPA language. We also have options for expanded audit and longer log retention as an add-on.
[04:44] Priya: One more technical: how do kernel selection and compilation work across different hardware? If we move models between H100 and A100, will perf vary a lot?
[04:52] Ethan: The runtime compiles and selects optimized kernels per hardware—perf does vary. H100 generally has better perf for transformer ops and larger KV caches, but A100 is still widely used. We can test on target hardware. The platform abstracts this so your API doesn't change when we route between variants.
[05:06] Carlos: What about throttling and rate limiting per token or per request? We need per-tenant quotas and RBAC.
[05:12] Maya: We support token-level rate limiting, per-route quotas, and RBAC tied into your SSO (SAML/SCIM). Tenant isolation is configurable with per-tenant pools.
[05:20] Priya: For an initial pilot, what's the timeline to get a dedicated pool up?
[05:24] Maya: From contract signature, typical lead time is 2–6 weeks depending on region and GPU availability. For EU Private or on-prem it's longer due to networking. We also offer a hosted pilot on reserved capacity quickly to validate.
[05:36] Ethan: If I may, I'll outline a proposed pilot: 2x A100 equivalent nodes reserved for two weeks, run Bench A with your prompt set (we'll capture p50/p95 latency and cost per 1k tokens), then propose scaled baseline. Does that align?
[05:48] Priya: Yes, that would be helpful.
[05:50] Carlos: One risk: vendor lock-in. If we want to move on-prem later, how portable is your setup?
[05:55] Maya: We aim to minimize lock-in—APIs are standard, model artifacts are yours, and we provide on-prem packages for Private deployments. There is operational work to migrate, but it's supported.
[06:04] Liam: Security question—are logs redacted? We need PII redaction support or a way to configure PII scrubbing pre-send.
[06:11] Ethan: We offer optional redaction pipelines and support customer-side scrubbing. For sensitive data we recommend sending minimal contexts or using client-side redaction, but we can also implement server-side scrubbers in the pipeline.
[06:21] Priya: For the benchmark, can we get measurements for both FP16 and Q4 quantized runs?
[06:25] Ethan: Yes we'll include both and highlight quality regressions observed.
[06:29] Carlos: Any other architectural notes for us?
[06:31] Ethan: One is caching—prefix and KV caching can drastically reduce compute. If you have many repeated prompts or long conversation context reused across requests, cache reuse reduces token compute. Also consider sharding users across pools to limit blast radius.
[06:42] Priya: Good point. We'll send our session characteristics.
[06:45] Maya: Ok quick recap of next steps: I'll send pricing and the dedicated tier matrix, Ethan will prepare a sizing + benchmark plan and we'll get sample prompts and traffic profile from Priya. We'll schedule the follow-up technical deep dive for week of 3/10.
[06:59] Carlos: Sounds good. Thanks for the run through.
[07:02] Liam: Thanks.
[07:04] Priya: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
